items.explanation: Correctness and prediction are explicitly separated in this unit: a system can be fully verified correct and still fall over under load nobody predicted, because verifying correctness and forecasting behavior under new conditions are different questions requiring different tools.

items.prompt: "Twice the users means twice the load" is an example of what kind of mistake, per this unit?
choices: A correctness bug — the code itself computes the wrong value for a given input
Linear intuition applied to non-linear reality — assuming a relationship is linear (proportional) when it's actually quadratic or exponential
A type error the compiler should have caught before the code ever shipped
An unrelated concept — user count and load are always exactly proportional to each other
items.explanation: This is the unit's named recurring failure mode: assuming a linear relationship (double the input, double the output) when the real relationship might be quadratic (every user talking to every other user) or exponential (compounding retries), and getting blindsided by how fast the wrong assumption breaks down.
items.reference:
Linear guess: 2x users → 2x load
Reality: could be quadratic (everyone talks to everyone) or exponential (compounding retries)

Why: intuition calibrated at small scale breaks silently at a bigger one.
items.learnMore:

Common mistake

Assuming the relationship you've observed at small scale is the same shape at 10x or 100x scale, without ever writing the actual relationship down.

items.prompt: A service handles 400 requests/second, each taking an average of 100ms end-to-end. Using Little's Law (L = λW), roughly how many concurrent requests should it be provisioned to handle?
choices: 400 — matching the requests-per-second figure directly
40 — computed as 400 × 0.1 seconds
4,000 — computed as 400 ÷ 0.1
It can't be estimated without knowing the server's CPU count
items.explanation: L = λW: average concurrent requests = arrival rate × average time in system = 400 × 0.1 = 40. This is exactly the kind of number that's easy to badly misjudge by intuition (guessing from '400 requests per second sounds like a lot') but is directly computable from two known quantities.
items.reference:
L = λW
concurrent = rate × time-in-system

Why: holds for any stable queueing system, regardless of arrival pattern shape.
items.learnMore:
Little's Law, worked

L = λW: average items in a system equals arrival rate times average time each item spends there.

SymbolMeaning
LAverage number of items in the system (what we solve for)
λAverage arrival rate
WAverage time each item spends in the system

Common mistake

Guessing concurrency directly from the requests-per-second figure alone ("400 req/s sounds like 400 concurrent") instead of multiplying by time-in-system.

items.explanation: L = λW: 5 tickets/minute × 20 minutes average time-in-system = 100 tickets open on average. Little's Law applies to any stable queueing system, not just web requests — a support queue works the same way.

items.prompt: Why does Little's Law apply equally to a web server's request queue, a support ticket backlog, and a factory production line?
choices: It doesn't really — Little's Law was originally derived for web servers and only loosely applies elsewhere
Because it holds for any stable queueing system regardless of the specific shape of the arrival pattern, which is what makes it broadly reusable
Because all three systems process exactly the same number of items per second
Because factories and web servers both run on the same kind of underlying scheduling software
items.explanation: Little's Law's generality comes from making very few assumptions — it holds for any stable queue regardless of how arrivals are distributed over time, which is exactly why the same L = λW relationship applies to requests, tickets, or physical items alike.
items.reference: Holds for any stable queueing system — web requests, tickets, factory items — regardless of the arrival pattern's shape.
items.learnMore:
Why Little's Law generalizes

Its power isn't a clever derivation for one specific system — it's that it makes almost no assumptions about how arrivals are distributed.

Common mistake

Assuming Little's Law only applies to web servers because that's the example used. It applies to any stable queue: support tickets, a factory line, a printer queue.

items.prompt: What does the "W" in Little's Law (L = λW) represent?
choices: The number of workers or servers currently available to process items
The average time each item spends in the system, from arrival to departure
The total number of items ever processed
The width of the queue's buffer, measured in number of available slots
items.explanation: W is the average time-in-system per item — how long an average request, ticket, or item stays in the system from arrival until it's done. Multiplied by the arrival rate λ, it gives L, the average number of items present at any moment.
items.reference: Holds for any stable queueing system — web requests, tickets, factory items — regardless of the arrival pattern's shape.

items.prompt: Per L2/L3's utilization curve, why is "we're at 60% utilization today, we can probably handle 90%" a risky plan?
choices: Because utilization can never legitimately rise above 60% in any well-run, properly provisioned system
Because wait time doesn't scale linearly with utilization near capacity — going from 60% to 90% utilization corresponds to roughly a 6x jump in relative wait time, not a proportional 1.5x jump
Because 90% utilization is always physically impossible for any real system to actually reach
Because the plan fails to separately account for network latency on top of queueing delay
items.explanation: Per the ρ/(1-ρ) approximation, wait time at 60% utilization is about 1.5x the 50% baseline, while at 90% it's about 9x — a 6x jump in wait time from a 1.5x jump in utilization. Linear intuition (utilization went up 50%, so wait time probably did too) badly undercounts the actual effect near saturation.
items.reference:
60% util1.5x wait
90% util9.0x wait

Why: a 1.5x utilization jump produces a 6x wait-time jump.
items.learnMore:
Why wait time isn't proportional to utilization

A busy server queues new arrivals behind an already-growing backlog, not just behind "the average case" — that compounding is what produces the non-linear shape.

UtilizationRelative wait (vs. 50%)
50%1.0x
60%1.5x
80%4.0x
90%9.0x
95%19.0x

Common mistake

Reading "we can handle 30% more utilization" as "we can handle roughly 30% more wait time." The same-sized utilization jump means wildly different wait-time jumps depending on where you start.

items.prompt: In the approximation relativeWaitTime(ρ) = ρ / (1 − ρ), what specifically causes the value to blow up as ρ approaches 1?
choices: The numerator ρ itself grows without bound as utilization keeps increasing toward 1
The denominator (1 − ρ) shrinks toward zero as ρ approaches 1, and dividing by a number approaching zero drives the result toward infinity
The formula is only an approximation and becomes invalid above ρ = 0.5
Floating-point rounding error accumulating during the calculation causes the apparent blowup
items.explanation: The numerator ρ stays bounded (it's a utilization fraction, never above 1), but the denominator (1 − ρ) shrinks toward zero as ρ → 1 — that shrinking denominator is exactly what drives the ratio toward infinity, which is the mathematical reason the wait-time curve gets steep near full capacity.
items.reference:
ρ / (1 − ρ)
as ρ → 1, denominator → 0, so the ratio → ∞

Why: the formula's shape *is* the blowup, not a separate description of it.
items.learnMore:
Why ρ/(1−ρ) blows up near ρ = 1

The denominator (1 − ρ) is what does the work: as utilization ρ approaches 1 (100% busy), (1 − ρ) shrinks toward 0, and dividing by a number approaching zero drives the whole expression toward infinity.

Common mistake

Treating the blowup as an empirical curiosity rather than reading it directly off the formula — the shape is fully explained by what happens to (1 − ρ) as ρ climbs.

items.prompt: At ρ = 0.5 (50% utilization), what does ρ / (1 − ρ) evaluate to, and why is this a natural baseline?
choices: 0 — because exactly half the system's capacity is sitting idle at that point
1 — because 0.5 / (1 − 0.5) = 0.5 / 0.5 = 1, giving a clean reference point that L2/L3's chart normalizes every other value against
0.5 — since the formula's output always matches the utilization value directly
Infinity — the formula is only mathematically undefined once ρ reaches exactly 0.5
items.explanation: 0.5 / (1 − 0.5) = 0.5 / 0.5 = 1 exactly, which is why 50% utilization is used as the "1.0x" reference baseline throughout L2/L3 — every other relative-wait-time figure is this raw formula value divided by this same baseline.

items.prompt: The capacity near-miss case study assumed per-request service time stays constant as traffic grows. Per L3, why is this assumption worth checking rather than accepting by default?
choices: It isn't worth checking — service time stays exactly constant regardless of how much load the system is under

In reality, contention effects (lock waiting, CPU scheduling, GC pauses under memory pressure) often make service time itself increase under load, compounding the utilization effect rather than staying independent of it
Service time only matters for CPU-bound workloads, not I/O-bound ones
The assumption is fine because Little's Law already accounts for changing service time automatically
items.explanation: L3's failure modes flag exactly this: assuming service time is constant under load is a real simplification that can hide additional risk, since contention effects often make service time itself worsen under load — a more careful prediction measures this rather than assuming it away.
items.reference:

Reality: contention (locks, scheduling, GC) often makes service time itself rise under load

items.learnMore:

Common mistake

Assuming service time is a fixed property of the code, rather than something that itself degrades under contention as load rises.

items.prompt: If service time itself rises as traffic grows (not just staying constant as the near-miss calculation assumed), what does that do to the projected utilization and wait-time figures?

It makes the real outcome better than projected, since slower service reduces load
It only affects average latency directly, leaving the utilization figure itself unchanged
items.explanation: Utilization is a function of both arrival rate and service time — if service time itself increases under load (due to contention), the resulting utilization (and the resulting wait-time blowup) is worse than a projection that held service time fixed, meaning the near-miss calculation's 9x figure could understate the real risk.

items.prompt: A flash sale is expected to cause a sharp, short traffic spike. Per L3's failure modes, is the steady-state utilization curve from L2/L3 the right tool to plan for it directly?

items.prompt: Per L3's failure modes, what's the correct relationship between a formula's prediction and real-world measurement?
choices: Once a formula produces a number, there's no further need to measure — the math is authoritative

The formula generates a specific, falsifiable expectation that should then be checked against real measurements — real systems have deviations from the formula's clean assumptions that only measurement can reveal

items.explanation: L3 explicitly warns against using the existence of a formula as an excuse to stop measuring reality — the correct use of predictive math is to generate a specific, falsifiable expectation and then check it against real measurements, not to treat the formula's output as ground truth on its own.

items.prompt: Implement `relativeWaitTime(utilization)`, the ρ/(1-ρ) queueing approximation from L3, where `utilization` is a number strictly between 0 and 1 (exclusive).

tests.description: wait time grows faster than utilization itself between 80% and 90%

items.explanation: This is the direct queueing approximation used throughout L2/L3: as utilization approaches 1 (100% busy), the denominator (1 - utilization) shrinks toward zero, which is exactly why wait time grows sharply rather than linearly as a system nears saturation — the formula's shape IS the non-linear blowup, not just a description of it.
items.reference: ρ / (1 − ρ) — as ρ → 1, denominator → 0, ratio → ∞
items.learnMore:
Implementing the wait-time formula

A one-line implementation, but the shape of the growth (not the line count) is the entire teaching point — the denominator shrinking toward zero as ρ approaches 1 is what produces the non-linear blowup, with no extra logic needed to make that happen.

items.prompt: Implement `estimateConcurrentRequests(requestsPerSecond, avgTimeInSystemSeconds)` using Little's Law (L = λW) from L2, returning the estimated average number of concurrent requests.

tests.description: 200 req/s at 150ms average gives 30 concurrent requests
400 req/s at 100ms average gives 40 concurrent requests
0 requests per second gives 0 concurrent requests
doubling the rate doubles the concurrency estimate, all else equal

items.explanation: Little's Law is a direct multiplication: average concurrent requests (L) equals the arrival rate (λ) times the average time each request spends in the system (W). Unlike the wait-time curve, this relationship IS linear in both of its inputs — the non-linearity in this unit comes from how W itself tends to grow as utilization rises, not from this formula.
items.reference: L = λW — concurrent = rate × time-in-system
items.learnMore:
Little's Law as code

This function is the entire L2 pseudocode example made concrete. Notice it's linear in both inputs — the interesting non-linearity in this unit lives in a separate formula (ρ/(1−ρ)) that predicts how W itself changes as a system nears saturation, not in Little's Law itself.
